tagline: From ranchland to Utah’s highest paved pass, then north past mountain lakes
intro: Mirror Lake Highway winds out of Kamas through farms and ranches, climbing into forested mountains with meadows and rugged peaks. This Forest Service Scenic Byway crosses an east-west mountain range, with overlooks, waterfalls, lakes and trailheads along the drive. Utah’s tourism office highlights the glacially carved valleys and alpine summits along the route. Access points along the highway lead into the High Uinta Wilderness. The route also offers picnic areas and campgrounds among its lakes and viewpoints.

The state legislature designated SR-150 in 1933, but that route ran only from Kamas to the national forest boundary. In 1953, the state extended the route east and north by way of Mirror Lake to the Wyoming line. The highway takes its name from the lake it passes. When the road closes to cars in winter, snowmobiles use it.

Begin on Center Street in Kamas, where the road heads east as a two-lane, undivided highway. The route passes through Samak before climbing to Bald Mountain Pass at 10,715 feet, the highest paved road in Utah. Beyond the crest, the descent passes Hayden Peak, Kletting Peak and Holiday Park Peak before the Wyoming border. The road continues north to the Wyoming border south of Evanston.
notice: Meadows interrupt the forested mountain terrain along the highway.

moments.title: Kamas
moments.text: Cattle ranching and lumber are Kamas’s main industries, at the town known as the Gateway to the Uinta Mountains. Its name comes from Camassia quamash, a regional flowering plant that Native Americans used for food. Here, Mirror Lake Highway begins at Main and Center streets and leaves town heading east. That first stretch passes farm and ranch land before rising into mountain forest. Kamas is also the starting point for the High Uintas Classic bicycle race, whose mountain stage crosses Bald Mountain Pass to Evanston. Travelers heading into the Uintas stop in town for supplies before entering the remote mountain wilderness.

moments.title: Mirror Lake
moments.text: Mirror Lake takes its name from reflections of the surrounding mountains and trees, visible from the shore or a roadside overlook. Water enters from Pass Lake just above it and leaves as the headwaters of the Duchesne River. Rainbow, brook and tiger trout inhabit the lake. The Forest Service owns the shoreline, with a campground, picnic facilities and a ramp for non-motorized boats. A 1.5-mile loop trail features the lake, gaining just 39 feet in elevation. Beside the campground, a day-use picnic area and a small boat ramp occupy the lake shore.
moments.notice: Mountains and trees are reflected in the lake, seen from the shore or roadside overlook.

moments.title: Hayden Peak
moments.text: The descent from Bald Mountain Pass goes past Hayden Peak before Kletting Peak and Holiday Park Peak. Hayden stands on the western edge of the High Uintas Wilderness, in the Uinta-Wasatch-Cache National Forest. Its name honors Ferdinand Hayden, the American geologist known for surveying expeditions in the Rocky Mountains in the late nineteenth century. The mountain supports mountain goats, pika and many wildflower species.

practical: Mirror Lake: The highway closes to automobiles in winter because of heavy snow. Driving the byway is free; using its recreation areas requires a fee pass. (checked 2026-10-11)
